extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in colonial politics, race, and abolitionist critique
extracted.subtask_description: A polemical essay rebutting the views of Mr. Froude on slavery, race, and West Indian self-government, arguing from historical fact, moral judgment, and lived experience. The piece evaluates rhetorical moves, factual accuracy, and political principles in Froude's writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid suppression of inconvenient facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The author condemns the deliberate omission or suppression of truth (e.g., adding or omitting 'or anywhere') used to make a policy appear tolerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppressing qualifying words or facts to make an argument more palatable is dishonest and logically futile; the author points to specific instances where Mr. Froude omits or alters phrases to mislead readers about the global situation of black populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical claims require concrete evidence, not insinuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions about past practices (for example, that planters had 'some organized method' for checking the coloured population's increase) must be supported by specific evidence rather than vague suggestion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask what the 'old lines' were and demand documentary or reliable testimony; avoid speculative or grotesque conjectures (the author mocks hypothetical methods like 'suffocation of the babes' or 'beetle-paste') used as rhetorical shock without proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge slavery by its actual phase and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery must be evaluated in the form it actually assumed—particularly its later plantation phase, which culminated in atrocities and became 'the sum ... of all human villainies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between archaic patriarchal servitude and the brutal plantation slavery of recent centuries; moral culpability hinges on real practices (capture, Middle Passage horrors, chains, lash, starvation), so glossing over these differences to reduce culpability is illegitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Societies legitimately adopt means of self-protection
rubrics_metrics.description: As 'self-defence is the first law of nature,' every organized society has recognized methods to guard against the unregulated assertion of 'average' human tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this principle to rebut arguments that portray all forms of social regulation as unjustified—recognize that some constraints evolve as protective social mechanisms, but beware using the idea to justify oppression without examination of means and ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical loaded words must fit authorial intention
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of an expletive like 'dangerously' can be 'critically allowable' insofar as it serves the author's main intention, but may be misleading if used to suggest truculence unjustifiably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether strong adjectives are being used to describe facts or to insinuate character judgments; the author permits emphatic language when it matches the argument but warns against suggestio falsi—implying falsehoods by tone rather than evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political authority should rest on competence and merit, not skin colour
rubrics_metrics.description: Governance and eligibility for office should be determined by intelligence, probity, and fitness, not by the colour of one's skin; 'no one can deserve to govern simply because he is white, and no one is bound to be subject simply because he is black.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples of cross-racial selection and cooperation to show that voters select competent representatives regardless of colour; rebut notions of race-based political entitlement or exclusion by demonstrating real-world instances where merit prevailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal opportunity produces equal distinguished men
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'no original or congenital difference of capacity' between races; with the same chances and treatment, distinguished men would be produced equally from both races.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims about political ineptitude or short tenure of office, apply the standard that equal training and opportunity should yield comparable outcomes (e.g., duration of tenure) across races; challenge arguments that deny this without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims about collective attitudes or reactions require substantiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements asserting how 'the blacks themselves would despise' a governor or that 'how long would such a connection endure' are empirical claims about attitudes and need supporting evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand sources or examples before accepting sweeping statements about what a population would feel or do; the author treats such blanket assertions as baseless and requiring demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and historical assertions about privileges must be accurate
rubrics_metrics.description: The contention that 'the exclusive privilege of colour over colour' existed as law in the British West Indies is refuted as false: 'Never in the history of the British West Indies ... was there any law or usage establishing superiority in privileges for any section ... on account of colour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify legislative and customary records before asserting racial legal privileges; avoid framing political history around false legal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lived experience and concrete examples to rebut generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The author relies on personal familiarity with many African tribes and on West Indian examples to contradict Mr. Froude's broad assertions about origins and condition of the enslaved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide names, demographic facts, and firsthand or documentary evidence to counter sweeping or abstract claims; empirical detail strengthens refutation of generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid romanticizing ancient or 'patriarchal' slavery to excuse modern abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoking patriarchal or theocratic forms of servitude to excuse or minimize modern plantation slavery's cruelties is illegitimate; ancient systems with household integration differ fundamentally from the commercialized, brutal trade and plantation regimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish historically between types of servitude; do not let descriptions of earlier regulated servitude be used to whitewash or relativize the crimes of recent slavery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalize from an unrepresentative minority to an entire 'race' or class
rubrics_metrics.description: The author criticizes Mr. Froude's tendency to treat a small malcontent 'handful' as if it represented the entire Anglo-Saxon race; such generalization is a grotesque facon de parler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating arguments that claim to speak for a whole group, check representativeness and scale; avoid allowing a small, atypical sample to dictate conclusions about a broad population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social classification should be by relevant qualities, not outward colour
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification in society (and science) should be based on affinity, ability, or circumstance (intellectual approximation, wealth, competence), not on skin colour—'no teacher marshals his pupils into classes according to any outward physical distinction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate policies and social orders by whether they group people by relevant performance or interest criteria rather than immutable physical traits; use analogies (horse/dog, teacher sorting by ability) to expose faulty racial taxonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose internal contradictions and hypocrisy in an opponent's argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The author repeatedly points out that Mr. Froude contradicts himself (e.g., praising sensible governors who rule black populations while denying blacks political fitness), using such contradictions to discredit his authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight and explain inconsistencies within an argument to weaken its persuasive power; show when an author’s claims in one passage undermine claims in another.
